finding.claim: The state-changing POST /settings/email endpoint is decorated with @login_optional instead of @login_required. Unauthenticated requests reach set_email() with g.uid = None, so the account-modifying operation is not protected by authentication. Depending on set_email's handling of a None uid (e.g. a WHERE uid IS NULL / unscoped update), an anonymous caller can change email for unintended accounts or trigger an error state. The sibling endpoint /settings/password correctly uses @login_required, which shows the intent was to require login. Email change is typically the first step of an account-takeover chain via password reset.
finding.source: Anonymous unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie.
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a protected account-modifying operation (the stub currently has no body; the real implementation is not in this repo).

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None for anonymous callers, and never aborts.
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with a possibly-None uid without any check.

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not applied here (it is applied on /settings/password at line 42). No inline `if g.uid is None: abort(401)` check. No before_request hook or global auth middleware. No CSRF protection (Flask-WTF/CSRFProtect) is present. set_email is a stub, so its internal None handling could not be verified. The app has no secret_key configured in this file, which may be set elsewhere.

verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None for anonymous callers without aborting (routes.py:22), and routes.py:37 calls set_email(g.uid, ...) with no check, unlike /settings/password's @login_required (routes.py:42), so an anonymous POST reaches the state-changing call; set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the impact beyond reachability is unverified.
